docs/owned-media.md: Social posts and video files remain owned assets even when distributed through rented platforms;
Social posts and video files can remain assets you control when distributed through rented platforms, subject to the rights you hold;
Owned media is any content you create and any channel you control — where no third party can revoke your access, change the rules, or take your audience away.

For operating purposes, distinguish content rights from practical control of distribution and audience relationships. Retain rights, permissions, exports, and migration options; a provider account is not a guarantee of uninterrupted access.
**The asset** (what you made) is always owned. A video file, a transcript, a clip, a written post — you created it, you own it, regardless of where it gets published.

**The asset** (what you made) is distinct from its distribution platform. Retain masters and confirm ownership or sufficient licenses, including contributor agreements and third-party components. Creating or uploading a file alone does not establish every right. The [U.S. Copyright Office](https://www.copyright.gov/what-is-copyright/) explains work-made-for-hire and ownership transfers; this is U.S. guidance, not a determination of any particular project’s rights.
Your website and email list are owned reach. LinkedIn and YouTube are rented reach.
A website and permissioned email list can provide more direct control; retain portable copies and check provider terms. Social-platform reach remains dependent on the platform.
This means social content you write and design is owned media. The platform you post it to is not. You own what you make. You do not own the pipe.
Treat social content as a reusable asset when you hold the necessary rights. That does not give you ownership of the distribution platform.
Raw outputs from a recording session. Owned before any platform touches them.
Raw outputs to retain from a recording session, subject to contributor agreements and the rights in incorporated material.
Everything created to wrap and surface the source media. Fully owned content regardless of where it's distributed.
Assets created to package the source media. Check reuse and distribution rights for each component.
These are the only channels where losing the platform means losing nothing — because you own the relationship.

These channels can improve continuity when you retain rights, audience permissions, independent exports, and a migration path. A hosting account still depends on its provider: [Transistor’s terms](https://transistor.fm/terms/) reserve account suspension or deletion.
you own the content, not the pipe
you retain content rights, not ownership of the platform
You own the content. You do not own the platform, the algorithm, or the audience relationship. If the platform disappears or changes its rules, the reach is gone.
Content rights and platform access are separate. A platform change can interrupt reach; independently retained, permissioned audience relationships may remain.
A channel termination or policy change would eliminate the audience relationship entirely. The video files themselves remain owned assets.

A channel termination or policy change can remove access to that platform audience; independently retained, permissioned relationships may remain. [YouTube’s terms](https://www.youtube.com/static?template=terms) preserve your existing content ownership while requiring upload rights and allowing service changes.
Data and reporting assets that live in your systems. Owned by definition.
Data and reporting assets to retain in your systems, subject to applicable permissions, contracts, and privacy requirements.
The longest-lived owned assets. These compound over time and power AI search discoverability (AEO).

Assets intended to support long-term retrieval and reuse. AI-search visibility must be measured rather than assumed; [Google’s guidance](https://developers.google.com/search/docs/appearance/ai-features) describes eligibility, not guaranteed inclusion.
What you create is always yours. Where it reaches is rented.
Check the rights in what you create separately from the conditions governing its distribution.
**Asset test:** Did you create it? → It's owned content.
**Asset test:** Do you own or hold sufficient rights to retain, reuse, and distribute it, including all incorporated components?
Owned media is built on assets you create and channels where you hold the relationship. Everything else is rented reach — valuable, but not yours.
Build around assets you have rights to use and relationships you can maintain with permission. Test exports and migration options instead of assuming that a platform account guarantees continuity.
